label: HMRC update · 18 November 2026
title: Payroll bureaus must register with HMRC as tax advisers by 17 February 2027
summary: Phase three of HMRC's tax adviser registration is open. Professionals who only provide payroll services for clients and do not have an agent services account must register by midnight on 17 February 2027.
body:
On 18 November 2026 HMRC opened phase three of its new tax adviser registration requirement, known as Modernising and Mandating Tax Adviser Registration. This phase is aimed at payroll professionals, and it matters both to payroll bureaus and to the businesses that use them.

Who needs to register in this phase

You need to register by midnight on 17 February 2027 if you:

  • solely provide professional third-party payroll services;
  • interact with HMRC on behalf of your clients; and
  • do not already have an agent services account (ASA).

HMRC says some payroll professionals may not think of themselves as tax advisers. Its position is that anyone paid to interact with HMRC on behalf of someone else is generally considered to be a tax adviser unless an exemption applies. Registration is free and online.

The four phases

  • 18 May 2026: unregistered advisers without an ASA who interact with HMRC for clients.
  • 18 August 2026: advisers with a Self Assessment or Corporation Tax account who do not have an ASA.
  • 18 November 2026: advisers who solely provide professional payroll services and do not have an ASA.
  • 31 December 2026: financial services organisations without an ASA.

HMRC says more than 5,000 new agent services accounts have been created since the first window opened. Advisers who already have an ASA do not need to register again. HMRC says they will be moved to the new digital service in the 2027 to 2028 financial year.

The conditions you must meet

HMRC's guidance, last updated on 18 November 2026, sets out conditions for the business and its relevant individuals. In summary:

  • Anti-money laundering: the business must have approved AML supervision in place before it applies. An application made without it will be rejected.
  • Tax affairs in order: no relevant outstanding returns or unpaid tax, unless covered by a payment plan.
  • No serious sanctions: for example no relevant unspent convictions for fraud or tax offences, no formal insolvency, and no ban from registering with HMRC.
  • Relevant individuals: where a business has 5 officers or fewer, all of them count. Where it has 6 or more, it identifies those who make strategic or management decisions about the tax work, with at least 5 in total.

HMRC usually checks the conditions after you apply and will contact you if it needs more information. It keeps checking after registration, and a registration may be suspended if the conditions stop being met.

What happens if you do not register

HMRC says it may limit an adviser's ability to act for clients, and that enforcement action, including financial penalties, is possible. Once you have applied and received a registration number, you can carry on dealing with HMRC while the application is processed.

What I would do now

  • Payroll bureaus: check whether you have an ASA. If not, confirm your AML supervision and register well before 17 February 2027.
  • Employers who outsource payroll: ask your payroll provider whether it is registered or has an ASA, so there is no disruption to RTI submissions or HMRC contact.
